title: Single cask bottlings explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What a single cask whisky is, why each release is limited and how to read a single cask label before you buy.
teaser: One cask, one bottling, no blending. That is why no two single cask releases taste the same.
standfirst: Most whisky is a mix of many casks, blended for consistency. A single cask bottling is the opposite: everything in the bottle came from one cask. Here is what that means, why the bottle count is small and what the label can tell you.
sections:
A single cask whisky is bottled from one individual cask, with no other cask mixed in. It is not the same as single malt. Single malt means malt whisky from one distillery, usually blended from many casks. A single cask bottling takes that further: one distillery, one cask.

Many single cask whiskies are also bottled at cask strength and without chill filtration, though not all. Our guide to whisky label terms sorts out the related words.

No two casks are the same. Oak varies from tree to tree. Casks have different histories, char levels and previous contents. They sit in different spots in the warehouse, where temperature and humidity differ. So two casks filled with the same spirit on the same day can taste noticeably different years later.

Blenders usually iron out that variation. A single cask release shows it off. That is the attraction for many drinkers. It is also the risk: you are buying one cask's personality, good or awkward.

It also means you cannot go back for more. When a single cask bottling sells out, that exact whisky is gone. A later release from the same distillery, even a cask filled the same week, will be a different whisky.
Why the bottle count is small

A cask only holds so much. Some of it has evaporated by the time it is emptied. An illustrative example: a 200 litre barrel loses part of its contents over the years and gives up perhaps 160 litres at bottling. At 70 centilitres a bottle, that is about 228 bottles, before any losses in filtering and filling.

A 500 litre sherry butt might give several hundred bottles. A small quarter cask, far fewer. That is why single cask labels often carry a bottle number such as 87 of 230.

Bottlers who reduce a single cask to a lower strength get more bottles from it, because water is added. Those releases are still single cask, just not cask strength. The label should tell you which.

• Cask number: the distillery's ID for that cask.
  • Cask type: ex-bourbon barrel, sherry butt, hogshead and so on. Our guide to maturation and casks explains each.
  • Distilled and bottled dates: tell you the age precisely.
  • Strength: often cask strength, so anywhere from the high 40s to over 60% ABV.
  • Bottle number and outturn: this bottle and how many the cask gave.

Not every label shows all of these. More detail usually means the bottler expects you to care about it.

Prices for single casks vary widely and reflect rarity as much as quality. A higher price is not a promise that you will like the whisky more.

Distilleries release single casks for special editions, visitor centres and clubs. Independent bottlers, firms that buy casks from distilleries and bottle them under their own labels, also release many single casks. Our guide to independent bottlers covers how that trade works.

Some distilleries also sell whole casks to private buyers, who bottle them later. Rules for owning and bottling a cask vary by country (and in India by state), so check the current position before considering one.

Because each cask is distinct, single cask tastings reward attention. Nose gently first, especially if the whisky is at cask strength. Taste a small sip neat, then add a few drops of water and try again. Look for what the cask added: vanilla and coconut from American oak, dried fruit and spice from sherry casks, drying tannin from European oak.

Comparing two single casks from the same distillery side by side is one of the clearest ways to see what a cask does. Pour small measures, keep water to hand, pace yourself and never drink and drive.

Indian distilleries have released single cask bottlings too. Warm Indian warehouses push casks hard, so the differences between casks can be large and arrive quickly. A single cask from an Indian warehouse can show deep colour and strong wood at an age that would be young in Scotland. Read the age and the cask type on the label together, rather than judging on age alone.

Single cask releases also need careful handling on the distillery side. Every bottle must trace back to the cask record, from fill date to final gauge, which is why distilleries with good cask records find single casks easier to release.

Next time you taste a single cask, write down the cask number, type, age and strength from the label, then three aromas and one word for the finish. After five or six entries you will start to see which cask types you prefer. That is worth more than any score in a magazine.
faqs: Is single cask the same as single malt?
No. Single malt is malt whisky from one distillery, usually blended from many casks. Single cask is bottled from one individual cask.
Why are single cask bottlings limited?
One cask only holds a few hundred litres at most, minus evaporation, so it yields a few hundred bottles.
Do single cask whiskies taste the same each release?
No. Every cask differs in wood, history and warehouse position, so each release has its own character.
